==Problem==
Alice has <imath>24</imath> apples. In how many ways can she share them with Becky and Chris so that each of the three people has at least two apples?

<imath>\textbf{(A) }105\qquad\textbf{(B) }114\qquad\textbf{(C) }190\qquad\textbf{(D) }210\qquad\textbf{(E) }380</imath>

==Solution 1 (Stars and Bars/Sticks and Stones)==

Note: This solution uses the non-negative version for stars and bars. A solution using the positive version of stars is similar (first removing an apple from each person instead of 2).

This method uses the counting method of stars and bars (non-negative version). Since each person must have at least <imath>2</imath> apples, we can remove <imath>2*3</imath> apples from the total that need to be sorted. With the remaining <imath>18</imath> apples, we can use stars and bars to determine the number of possibilities. Assume there are <imath>18</imath> stars in a row, and <imath>2</imath> bars, which will be placed to separate the stars into groups of <imath>3</imath>. In total, there are <imath>18</imath> spaces for stars <imath>+ 2</imath> spaces for bars, for a total of <imath>20</imath> spaces. We can now do <imath>20 \choose 2</imath>. This is because if we choose distinct <imath>2</imath> spots for the bars to be placed, each combo of <imath>3</imath> groups will be different, and all apples will add up to <imath>18</imath>. We can also do this because the apples are indistinguishable. <imath>20 \choose 2</imath> is <imath>190</imath>, therefore the answer is <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(C) }190}</imath>.
 

~goofytaipan91

==Solution 2 (Answer Choices)==
Consider an unordered triple <imath> (a,b,c) </imath> where <imath> a+b+c=24 </imath> and <imath> a,b,c </imath> are not necessarily distinct. Then, we will either have <imath> 1 </imath>, <imath> 3 </imath>, or <imath> 6 </imath> distinguishable ways to assign <imath> a </imath>, <imath> b </imath>, and <imath> c </imath> to Alice, Becky, and Chris. Thus, our answer will be <imath> x+3y+6z </imath> for some nonnegative integers <imath> x,y,z </imath>. Notice that we only have <imath> 1 </imath> way to assign the numbers <imath> a,b,c </imath> to Alice, Becky, and Chris when <imath> a=b=c </imath>. As this only happens <imath> 1 </imath> way (<imath>a=b=c=8</imath>), our answer is <imath> 1+3y+6z </imath> for some <imath> y,z </imath>. Finally, notice that this implies the answer is <imath> 1 </imath> mod <imath> 3 </imath>. The only answer choice that satisfies this is <imath> \boxed{\textbf{(C) }190} </imath>. 

-BorealBear

==Solution 3==
Since each person needs to have at least two apples, we can simply give each person two, leaving <imath> 24 - 2\times3=18 </imath> apples. For the remaining apples, if Alice is going to have <imath> a </imath> apples, Becky is going to have <imath> b </imath> apples, and Chris is going to have <imath> c </imath> apples, we have indeterminate equation <imath> a+b+c=18 </imath>. Currently, we can see that <imath> 0 \leq a\leq 18 </imath> where <imath> a </imath> is an integer, and when <imath> a </imath> equals any number in the range, there will be <imath> 18-a+1=19-a </imath> sets of values for <imath> b </imath> and <imath> c </imath>. Thus, there are <imath> 19 + 18 + 17 + \cdots + 1 = \boxed{\textbf{(C) }190} </imath> possible sets of values in total.

~[[User:Bloggish|Bloggish]]
